chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the man who has with him only the provision for his day: Should he give preference to the one who has the provision for his day over the one who has nothing, and should he give preference to the one who has the provision for a month over the one who has less than it, and the year in a similar manner, or is all of that the sufficiency (kafaf) for which he is not blamed?

So he (peace be upon him) said: It is a matter wherein the best of you is the one most eager for preferring (others) over himself, for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'And they give preference over themselves, even though poverty may afflict them.'
And the other matter is that he is not blamed for sufficiency (kafaf), and the higher hand is better than the lower hand, and begin with those whom you support.

key_terms.الْأَثَرَةِ: Preference / Giving preference to others over oneself
key_terms.الْكَفَافُ: Sufficiency / The level of provision that exempts one from blame

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between sufficiency (kafaf) and preferring others (ithar) in Islamic charity and family support?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between the legal baseline of 'kafaf' (sufficiency), where one is not blamed for providing only enough for oneself and dependents, and the spiritual excellence of 'ithar' (preferring others), which is a voluntary act of virtue. He cites the Quranic principle of the Ansar to illustrate that true superiority lies in self-sacrifice even in scarcity, while affirming that the 'upper hand' (giver) is superior to the 'lower hand' (receiver). This hadith establishes a nuanced hierarchy in Shia ethics, encouraging believers to transcend mere obligation and emulate the generosity of the Prophet's companions.

en.hubeali: A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Khalid, from Usman Bin Isa, from Sama’at who said,

‘I asked Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> about the man who does not have with him except for his provision for his day. Can the one who has his provision for his day with him be sympathetic towards the one who does not have anything, and can the one who has provisions for a month be sympathetic upon the one who has less than it, and the year is upon approximate to that, or is all of that the subsistence which he cannot be blamed over it?’

So heasws said: ‘It is such a matter that the most superior of you in it is the one most desirous upon the preferring (others) upon himself, for Allahazwj Mighty and Majestic is Saying [59:9] and prefer (them) before themselves though poverty may afflict them.
And the other matter is that he cannot be blamed upon the subsistence, and the higher (providing) hand is better than the lower (receiving) hand, and begin with the ones dependant (upon you)’.
en.sarwar: 1. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from ibn Khalid from ‘Uthman from ibn ‘Isa from Sama‘ah, who has said the following: “I once asked abu ‘ Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, this question: ‘There is one who has sustenance for only one day, or for only one month or one year. Should he give preference to another person who does not have sustenance even for one day, or one month or one year, or in all cases, is there no blame in not giving preference because of sustenance being barely enough for himself? 5

He (the Imam) said, ‘There are two issues. Those of you who are more inclined to giving preference to others over themselves are excellent. Allah, the Most Majestic, the Most Glorious, has said, “They give preference to others over themselves even though they themselves are in dire need.” [59:9]

The other issue is that in not giving preference to others over themselves, they are not blamed; however, a providing hand has the upper hand over a non-providing hand, but you must begin with your dependents.’”
